problem:
Harbour Energy collects monthly direct debits from customers across several SEPA countries, and the billing team plans its collections on a single calendar: the creditor's own business calendar. In a recent month, a collection due on a public holiday in the debtor's country was debited a day late, and another collection due on a day the clearing system was closed was submitted on the wrong day and rejected. The billing team assumed that one calendar, the creditor's, governed every milestone. It does not. The submission deadline, the inter-PSP settlement date and the debtor debit date are each governed by a different calendar, and each participant can be closed on a different day.

The calendars in play are the creditor PSP's business calendar, the debtor PSP's business calendar, the clearing and settlement mechanism's calendar, and the TARGET calendar for euro settlement. A date that is a business day for the creditor PSP may be a holiday for the debtor PSP, and a date that is a business day for both PSPs may be a day when the clearing system is closed. SDD Core uses the Inter-PSP Business Day definition, and the submission deadline of D-1 is one Inter-PSP Business Day before the due date, so the calculation depends on which days count as business days for the participants involved.

Harbour Energy needs a date-calculation service that applies the right calendar to each milestone, retains the calendar version used, and moves due dates and submission dates explicitly when a calendar makes the planned date invalid, rather than letting the payment fail at the clearing system or debit late without explanation.
solution:
Build a calendar service that holds separate calendars for the creditor PSP, the debtor PSP, the clearing and settlement mechanism and TARGET, each versioned with effective dates. For every collection, the service calculates each milestone against its governing calendar: the submission date from the D-1 Inter-PSP Business Day rule, the inter-PSP settlement date from the clearing calendar, and the debtor debit date from the debtor PSP calendar. The calculation records the calendar version used, so any date can be reproduced and audited later.

Apply explicit adjustment rules and communicate the result. When a planned due date is not a business day for the relevant participant, move the date under the scheme's adjustment rule and tell the customer the revised date in the pre-notification, so the customer is never surprised by a debit on a different day. When a calendar is updated after scheduling, recheck every scheduled collection against the new version and report what changed. Never use one generic bank-holiday calendar for the whole chain, because that is the error that caused the late debit and the rejected submission.

Test the service with a calendar matrix: a collection due on a creditor holiday, a debtor holiday, a clearing closure, and a date that is valid everywhere, plus a calendar update published after scheduling. For each case, assert the submission date, the settlement date and the debit date, and assert that the customer notice and the ledger both show the adjusted dates.

decision.question: You are the business analyst for Harbour Energy. Collections are planned on the creditor's calendar only. A collection due on a holiday in the debtor's country debited late, and another was rejected because the clearing system was closed on the planned submission day. The operations director asks for your recommendation.

options.label: A
options.detail: Ask the debtor PSPs to stay open on their national holidays.

options.label: B
options.detail: Move all collections to the first business day of the month to avoid holiday calculations.

options.label: C
options.detail: Keep using the creditor's calendar for all milestones and let any failures be handled as exceptions.

options.label: D
options.detail: Calculate each milestone against its governing calendar, retain the calendar version used, and adjust due and submission dates explicitly where a planned date is invalid.

decisionRationale: Option D is correct because each milestone has its own governing calendar, and only a per-milestone calculation with a retained calendar version produces correct submission, settlement and debit dates. Option C guarantees repeat failures. Option B moves every collection and breaks the customers' billing expectations. Option A is not within the creditor's control.

steps.title: Plans the monthly collection with a planned due date
Calculates the submission date, settlement date and debit date using the governing calendar for each milestone
Adjusts the due date where the planned date is not a business day for the relevant participant
Generates the collection file with the adjusted dates
Validates the file and submits it by the D-1 deadline computed on the Inter-PSP Business Day calendar
Routes the collection and settles the interbank position on a day the clearing system is open
Debits the debtor account on the due date under the debtor PSP calendar
Reconciles collections against the adjusted dates and the calendar version used

happy: The planned due date is checked against the creditor PSP, clearing and debtor PSP calendars, the submission date is calculated as D-1 on the Inter-PSP Business Day calendar, and the settlement and debit dates satisfy their governing calendars. The collection is submitted on time, settles on the planned day and is debited on the due date, with the calendar version used recorded for audit.

negative.title: Unexpected national holiday
negative.detail: A holiday is declared after collections have been scheduled. Recheck all scheduled collections against the new calendar, adjust the affected dates, and notify the affected customers of any revised due date.

negative.title: Calendar update after scheduling
negative.detail: The clearing system publishes a revised calendar and previously valid dates are no longer valid. Store the calendar version with every calculation, and re-run the calculation when a new version is published, with a report of what changed.

negative.title: Timezone boundary
negative.detail: A due date falls on different calendar days for participants in different timezones. Use the governing calendar for each milestone rather than a single timezone, and state the date and the timezone in every customer-facing message.

negative.title: Submission day falls on a clearing closure
negative.detail: The planned submission date is a day the clearing system is closed. Hold the collection to the next valid submission day, recalculate the due date, and tell the customer the revised date rather than submitting on a closed day.

technical: Hold each participant calendar as a versioned data set with effective dates, and never merge them into one generic holiday list. Store the calendar version alongside every date calculation so the result is reproducible. Compute dates per milestone against the governing calendar, and keep the original planned date, the adjusted date and the adjustment reason in the record. Use correlation IDs to link the calendar calculation, the collection instruction, the interbank message and the ledger entry. Schedule a recheck job that runs whenever a calendar version is published, and report the collections it changes. Test with a calendar matrix covering creditor, debtor and clearing closures, timezone boundaries and post-scheduling updates.

accounting: A collection whose due date is moved because of a calendar difference is value-dated on the adjusted date, and the ledger must reflect the adjusted date, not the originally planned one. Collections that cannot settle on the planned date are reported as calendar-held items, and the customer statement shows the actual debit date. Operations works from a calendar-exception worklist, and Finance tracks the value of collections rescheduled for calendar reasons each month. A settlement that was expected on a day the clearing system was closed must be reconciled against the next settlement date, with the break explained as a calendar difference rather than a missing payment.
